date: undated Geniza letter (PGP gives no date; classical Geniza period, 11th-13th c., is plausible for a Qus-Fustat family letter but is not assessed)
title: Son in Qus to his mother: Judaeo-Arabic letter with six lines in a secret language (nearly every word begins with alef)
correspondents: a son in Qus -> his mother, presumably in Fustat
folio_note: recto, about 17 lines in Hebrew script; lines 7-12 (six lines, about 30 words) are the secret passage, written in ordinary Hebrew letters; verso is a second letter in Arabic script mixed with Hebrew script
status: PGP: "Written in Judaeo-Arabic and a cipher (lines 7-12; noticed by OZ; probably this is also in Judaeo-Arabic) ... Needs examination/decipherment"; tags cipher, to examine. PGP shows no transcription. This is the letter Elbaum's 2022 Genizah blog describes (found by Oded Zinger; almost all words begin with alef, so not a plain substitution). Not on DECODE.
why: The only Geniza family letter known with an unread secret-language passage; the clear lines around it give the context (regards, a complaint about Abu Mansur).
verify: Transcribe lines 7-12 from the JTS image (5428 x 7230 px); test word-game hypotheses (alef prefixed to each word or syllable, letter shift after a dummy alef); ask O. Zinger / A. Elbaum (Princeton Geniza Project) whether a reading is in hand.

seen.cipher: Ordinary Hebrew square/semi-cursive letters, same hand and pen as the clear Judaeo-Arabic lines above and below, but the words are not Judaeo-Arabic words and most of them begin with alef. No interlinear or marginal gloss on the leaf; the verso (a second letter, Arabic and Hebrew script) carries no key or reading.

prior_art.literature: Elbaum, Cambridge Genizah Research Unit blog, 22 Jun 2022: Zinger's letter has "a portion in an incomprehensible cipher. Almost all the words begin with alef". Bohak 2010 (CSIC) treats a different cipher; T-S NS 70.1 (cracked by Bohak 2025, unpublished) was viewed and is a different system (dotted Hebrew-letter substitution).

vetting.key_check: No key is known for this system. The Geniza keys on record (CUL Or.1080 J277: Coptic-numeral, atbash and pangram keys; T-S K2.4 atbash) are letter substitutions and do not produce alef-initial words; not tested by hand in this sweep, which does not solve.

date: after 1 Nisan 1139 (inferred, PGP / India Book IV)
title: Yishaq b. Avraham Ibn Ezra to Halfon b. Netanel ha-Levi: Judaeo-Arabic letter with three words in a Coptic-numeral code
correspondents: Yishaq b. Avraham Ibn Ezra (Spain) -> Halfon b. Netanel ha-Levi
language: Judaeo-Arabic (Hebrew script), code in Greek/Coptic numerals
shelfmark: Cambridge University Library, T-S 13J18.19 (India Book IV, 41 = H55; PGPID 9097)
folio_note: recto line 11 (five numeral signs after 'wa-l-'), recto line 12 (three signs at the line start), verso line 5 (about 11 signs, readings doubtful); paper 16.9 x 25.1 cm
status: Edited: Gil and Fleischer, Yehuda ha-Levi and his Circle (2001) pp. 282-285, who proposed readings for the first two code words by two different methods and none for the third; Goitein, Friedman and Ashur, India Book IV B (2013) no. 41 print the signs and judge the matter unresolved (PGP: "substitution mechanism that has not yet been determined"). Partial, disputed proposals in print: no vetting block. Not on DECODE.
why: A dated 1139 Andalusi merchant-scholar letter (Halfon / Judah ha-Levi circle) hiding names or goods in a numeral code; the oldest dated unread Judaeo-Arabic code found.
verify: Read Gil-Fleischer pp. 282-285 and India Book IV B no. 41 note 1 for the proposed solutions; test the Coptic-numeral letter keys of CUL Or.1080 J277 verso, Bodl. MS heb. f 102/28 and JRL L 259 on the three groups; too short for anything but a key test.
prior_art: partial proposals in print, disputed (Gil-Fleischer 2001 pp. 282-285; India Book IV B no. 41 leaves it open); checked 15 Nov 2026 on PGP only, the two books not opened
